1275.title: Pure Land, closed
1275.hook: a vow, a name, a sunset, a land of light
1275.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists call Amitabha's name, Namu Amida Butsu in Japan and Namo Amituofo in China, in temple services, at home, with the dying, and in gratitude, trusting the vow of a Buddha of infinite light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many views of the land: a real place in the west, a mind made pure, or both, with the name shared by all. Your line was more than one answer.

A vow. A name. A sunset. A land of light. If the Pure Land fit on a postcard, those four would be the picture. A monk long ago makes vows so large they need a whole world to hold them. A buddha's name becomes something anyone can say: a farmer, a queen in prison, a clog-maker at his bench. The sun goes down in the west like a drum hung in the sky. And beyond it lies a land where even the birds teach. Today: Pure Land.
screen: `A VOW. A NAME.` → `A SUNSET. A LAND OF LIGHT.` → `PURE LAND.`

segments.voice: First, the vow. It began with Sukhavati, the land of bliss, and the monk Dharmakara, who in the Larger Sukhavati-vyuha makes his great vows. At their heart is the primal vow: that anyone who calls his name with trust will be born in his land. Dharmakara becomes Amitabha, the Buddha of infinite light and infinite life. Second, the land and the seeing. The Smaller sutra described the jeweled trees and the birds that teach. Then Queen Vaidehi, locked away by her own son, asked for a land without sorrow, and the Buddha taught her to see it: the setting sun, then water, ice and crystal ground. Third, the name: Namu Amida Butsu, Namo Amituofo. Tanluan and Shandao shaped the practice in China. In Japan, Shinran spoke of other power, tariki, and of shinjin, true entrusting, with the name said in gratitude. Rennyo carried it to farmers in simple letters. In China and Vietnam, people sit and call the name together. At the deathbed, the name is said with the dying. And the myokonin, like Saichi the clog-maker, lived it with quiet joy. Fourth, the land today: temples far from Asia, some called churches; teachers who say the land is also a mind made pure here; and more than one answer about what the land is, held side by side. What runs through all of it is light. Amitabha's name means infinite light, and the tradition holds that this light leaves no one out. Tomorrow a new part begins: the traditions of Tibet.
screen: `THE VOW: DHARMAKARA BECOMES AMITABHA.` · `THE LAND: TREES, BIRDS, A SETTING SUN.` · `THE NAME: SAID IN TRUST AND THANKS.` · `THE LAND TODAY: HERE, THERE, BOTH.` · then, large: `INFINITE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you say the nembutsu, say it now, once or a few times, Namu Amida Butsu or Namo Amituofo, slowly, and then stop; if you don't, hold the words infinite light in mind for one breath. Then rest, and let the light, whatever it means to you, do the rest of the sitting.
Pure Land. The tradition of Amitabha Buddha: a vow, a name said with trust, a land of light in the west and, for some teachers, a mind made pure here. Today's word.
Your line: infinite light. A vow, a name, a sunset, a land of light. That's the Pure Land, whole.

1276.title: The diamond vehicle, deeper
1276.hook: the Vajrayana builds on the Mahayana with tantra, ritual and a close bond with a teacher
1276.howItsDone: Vajrayana Buddhists in Tibet, the Himalayas and beyond practice mantra, mandala and visualization, often using a vajra and bell in ritual, and receive practices in person from a teacher through empowerments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Pure Land closed: a vow, a name, a sunset, a land of light. Your line was infinite light.

On a low table in a Tibetan shrine room sit two small objects. One is a short metal scepter, pinched in the middle and flaring out at both ends like two closed flowers. The other is a hand bell. A practitioner picks up the scepter in the right hand and the bell in the left, crosses the wrists, and rings. The scepter is called a vajra, and it gives a whole way of Buddhism its name. Today: the diamond vehicle, deeper.
screen: `A SCEPTER AND A BELL.` → `THE VAJRA NAMES A WHOLE WAY.` → `THE DIAMOND VEHICLE, DEEPER.`

segments.voice: First, what it builds on. You walked a little way down this path in year one; now, further in. The Vajrayana doesn't throw out what came before. Its aim is the Mahayana aim: to wake up for the sake of all beings. Bodhicitta, compassion and emptiness all stay underneath, Tibetan teachers say. What changes is the method. Vajra is usually rendered as diamond, or thunderbolt: something that can't be broken, and something that strikes fast. So the diamond vehicle presents itself as a strong, quick way to the same awakening. Second, tantra. The word names a family of texts and the practices they teach: mantra, the sacred sound, like Om mani padme hum from year one; mandala, the sacred map, like the sand mandala swept into the river; and visualization, where a practitioner pictures a buddha or a figure like Tara so clearly that, in the teaching, the line between seer and seen begins to soften. Third, ritual. Body, speech and mind are all put to work: the hands hold the vajra and the bell, or make gestures called mudras; the voice chants; the mind holds the image. Nothing about a person is left out of practice. Fourth, the teacher. In the Vajrayana the bond with a teacher, a lama or guru, is close and central. Teachings are given in person, often through an empowerment, a ceremony that opens a practice to the student. That's why Tibetan teachers themselves warn students to check a teacher carefully, for a long time, before trusting. The bell in the left hand, the vajra in the right: wisdom and method, held together.
screen: `BUILT ON THE MAHAYANA.` · `TANTRA: MANTRA, MANDALA, VISUALIZATION.` · `BODY, SPEECH AND MIND AT WORK.` · `A CLOSE BOND WITH A TEACHER.` · then, large: `THE DIAMOND VEHICLE.`

segments.voice: Think back to your year-one Tibetan weeks: the mantra of Chenrezig, prayer flags in the wind, tonglen, breathing in someone's pain and breathing out relief, Tara who comes quickly, the sand mandala swept away. Let one of them come back on its own, and stay with it. If it's a mantra, let it sound quietly in your mind; if it's an image, let it sit in front of you.
Vajrayana. The diamond vehicle: the Buddhism of Tibet and the Himalayas, built on the Mahayana, with tantra, ritual and a close bond with a teacher. Today's word.
Your line: the diamond vehicle. Wisdom and method, held together. See you tomorrow.

1277.title: Three vehicles, one path
1277.hook: Tibetans describe practicing all three vehicles together: renunciation, compassion, and the diamond path
1277.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists describe practicing three vehicles together, renunciation and ethics, the compassion of the bodhisattva, and the methods of tantra, and monastics may keep the vows of all three at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vajrayana: the vajra in one hand, the bell in the other, tantra, ritual and a close bond with a teacher. Your line was the diamond vehicle.

A Tibetan monk gets dressed in the morning. The robes he puts on carry the vows of a monk: no killing, no stealing, a simple life. Before breakfast he recites a prayer to wake up for the sake of every living being. Later, in the shrine room, he picks up the vajra and the bell and chants a mantra. Three things in one morning, and to him they aren't three separate religions or even three separate schools. They're three layers of one practice, stacked like the floors of a house. Today: three vehicles, one path.
screen: `A MONK'S MORNING.` → `THREE LAYERS, ONE HOUSE.` → `THREE VEHICLES, ONE PATH.`

segments.voice: First, the word vehicle. In Sanskrit it's yana, something that carries you. Buddhist texts speak of more than one vehicle toward awakening. Tibetan teachers describe three, and their point is that one person can ride all three at once. Second, the foundation: renunciation. The first vehicle, as Tibetans frame it, is about seeing clearly that grasping brings suffering, and turning away from it: ethics, simplicity, the vows of personal liberation, the four thoughts that turn the mind from year one. A word of care: this layer has sometimes been given a name that sounds like lesser, and Theravada Buddhists, who follow the way of the elders, describe their own path in their own terms and don't use that name for themselves. In the Tibetan scheme, the first vehicle names a layer inside every practitioner, not someone else's school. Third, the great vehicle: compassion. On top of renunciation sits bodhicitta, the wish to wake up not for yourself alone but for all beings, and the wisdom that sees things as empty of a fixed self. Tonglen and mind training live here. Fourth, the diamond vehicle. On top of both sit the methods of tantra: mantra, visualization, the bond with a teacher. Tibetan teachers say this top floor stands on the lower ones, and without them it falls. That's why a monk can keep the vows of a monk, the vows of a bodhisattva and the commitments of tantra all at the same time.
screen: `YANA: SOMETHING THAT CARRIES YOU.` · `THE FOUNDATION: RENUNCIATION.` · `THE GREAT VEHICLE: COMPASSION.` · `THE DIAMOND PATH, ON TOP OF BOTH.` · then, large: `ALL THREE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Take the three one at a time, a breath for each. Renunciation: loosen your grip a little on one thing you hold too tightly. Compassion: wish one person well. The diamond path: let a mantra, if you have one, or a quiet hum rest in your chest; then hold all three together, as one breath.
Three vehicles. In Tibetan teaching, renunciation, compassion and the diamond path, practiced together as layers of one path, each standing on the one below. Today's word.
Your line: all three at once. Three floors, one house. Same time tomorrow.

1278.title: Nyingma
1278.hook: the "ancient" school tracing back to Padmasambhava
1278.howItsDone: Nyingma Buddhists honor Padmasambhava, Guru Rinpoche, as the source of their lineage, practice the Dzogchen teachings, and include both monastics and lay yogis called ngakpas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three vehicles, one path: renunciation, compassion and the diamond path, stacked like the floors of a house. Your line was all three at once.

A figure sits on a lotus in paintings on temple walls across the Himalayas. He wears a red hat with a feather on top, a curling mustache, and wide, steady eyes that seem to look straight through the wall. A tall staff rests in the crook of one arm. Tibetans call him Guru Rinpoche, the precious teacher. Tradition says he came to Tibet from India, met the forces that blocked the teaching, and won them over. The ancient school of Tibet traces itself back to him. Today: Nyingma.
screen: `A FIGURE ON A LOTUS, A FEATHERED HAT.` → `GURU RINPOCHE, THE PRECIOUS TEACHER.` → `NYINGMA.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Nyingma is usually translated as the ancient ones, or the old school. It looks back to the early wave of teaching in Tibet, when Indian teachers and Tibetan translators brought the sutras and tantras over the mountains. Schools that formed later were sometimes called the new ones, and the Nyingma kept the older translations as their own. Second, Padmasambhava, whom you met in year three. His name is usually rendered lotus-born, and tradition says he appeared as a child sitting in a lotus on a lake. In the Nyingma story, a Tibetan king invited him, and he helped build the monastery at Samye, taming the spirits of the land so the walls built by day would stop falling down at night. Whether a listener takes that as history, as teaching, or both, the Nyingma remember him as the one who planted the diamond vehicle in Tibetan ground. Third, Dzogchen. Nyingma teachers hold up Dzogchen, the great perfection, as the heart of their path: the mind's own nature is already open, clear and awake, and practice is learning to rest in it rather than build it. Fourth, the shape of the school. The Nyingma have great monasteries, and also a long line of lay practitioners called ngakpas, who may marry, keep homes, grow their hair long, and still carry the full practice. The ancient ones were never only behind monastery walls. They lived in villages and on farms too.
screen: `NYINGMA: THE ANCIENT ONES.` · `PADMASAMBHAVA, THE LOTUS-BORN.` · `DZOGCHEN, THE GREAT PERFECTION.` · `MONASTERIES, AND VILLAGE YOGIS.` · then, large: `THE ANCIENT ONES.`

segments.voice: Picture Padmasambhava in front of you, a little above eye level: the lotus beneath him, the red hat and feather, the steady eyes, the staff in the crook of his arm. You don't have to believe anything about him to do this; just let the picture be clear and calm. Then let it slowly fade, and rest in whatever is left: open, quiet, awake.
Nyingma. The ancient school of Tibetan Buddhism, tracing itself to Padmasambhava and the early translations, with Dzogchen, the great perfection, at its heart. Today's word.
Your line: the ancient ones. In monasteries, and in villages too. Until tomorrow.

1279.title: Hidden treasures
1279.hook: Nyingma teachings said to be hidden and later found by treasure-revealers
1279.howItsDone: Nyingma Buddhists practice from terma, treasure teachings said to have been hidden by Padmasambhava and Yeshe Tsogyal and revealed later by tertons, alongside the teachings passed down without interruption from teacher to student.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nyingma, the ancient school, with Padmasambhava on his lotus and Dzogchen at its heart. Your line was the ancient ones.

A rider stops at the foot of a cliff in eastern Tibet. He has seen this place before, he says, in a dream. He climbs to a crack in the rock, reaches in, and draws out a small box. Inside is a roll of yellow paper covered in signs no one around him can read. He wraps it carefully and tells almost nobody. Months later, maybe years, he sits down and begins to write out a whole teaching from it. That, in the Nyingma telling, is how a hidden treasure comes to light. Today: hidden treasures.
screen: `A CLIFF FROM A DREAM.` → `A SMALL BOX, A YELLOW SCROLL.` → `HIDDEN TREASURES.`

segments.voice: First, the word, which you met in year three, in Tibet's dark years. Terma means treasure, and in the Nyingma school it names teachings hidden on purpose, to be found later. Tradition says Padmasambhava and his close disciple Yeshe Tsogyal hid many teachings across Tibet, because the people then weren't ready for them; they were meant for a later age that would need them. Second, where treasures hide. Some are earth treasures, sealed in rocks, lakes, statues or pillars, like the box in the cliff. Others are mind treasures, hidden, the tradition says, in the deep mind of a disciple, to rise up whole in a later life. The scrolls are often said to be written in a coded script that only one person can read. Third, the treasure-revealer, called a terton. Tradition says a terton is a disciple of Padmasambhava reborn, with a seal on the mind that opens at the right time and place. Revealing a treasure isn't treated as easy or safe: a terton may wait for signs, keep the find secret, and check it with other teachers. Fourth, what came out of the ground. Tradition holds that the text often called the Tibetan Book of the Dead, read aloud to the dying, which you met in year one as the bardo teachings, is a treasure revealed this way. Some readers take terma as literal finds, some as visionary revelation, some as both. What the Nyingma stress is the idea underneath: teaching that waits until someone needs it.
screen: `TERMA: TEACHINGS HIDDEN ON PURPOSE.` · `EARTH TREASURES AND MIND TREASURES.` · `THE TERTON, WHO KNOWS WHEN.` · `WHAT WAITS UNTIL IT'S NEEDED.` · then, large: `HIDDEN TREASURE.`

Turn it over once, the way a terton might unroll a scroll, then hold it quietly, as if it had waited for today.

1280.title: Kagyu
1280.hook: the lineage of Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa
1280.howItsDone: Kagyu Buddhists trace their practice through Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, receive teachings in person from a teacher, and sing Milarepa's songs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, terma: teachings hidden on purpose, found by treasure-revealers when the time was right. Your line was hidden treasure.

A scholar sits reading at a great monastery in India, with books stacked around him. A shadow falls across the page. An old woman, bent and ugly in the story, is standing over him. She asks whether he understands the words. He says yes, and she laughs with delight. She asks whether he understands the meaning. He says yes again, and she bursts into tears. You understand the words, she tells him, but not the meaning. The scholar is Naropa. He puts down his books and goes looking for a teacher. Today: Kagyu.
screen: `A SHADOW FALLS ACROSS THE PAGE.` → `THE WORDS, BUT NOT THE MEANING.` → `KAGYU.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Kagyu is often rendered the lineage of oral instruction, and some call it the whispered lineage: teaching passed by mouth, from a teacher to a student who is ready, one link at a time. Second, the Indian links. Tilopa, in the story, was a wild yogi with no monastery at all. Naropa found him and served him through a long run of hard and strange trials before Tilopa gave him the teaching. Tradition says Tilopa finally struck him on the head with a sandal, and Naropa woke up. Third, the bridge to Tibet. Marpa was a Tibetan farmer and family man, with a wife and a household, who crossed the mountains to India more than once to study with Naropa, carrying gold to offer and texts to bring home. He's remembered as Marpa the Translator. Fourth, the student no one would have picked, whom you met in year three. Milarepa, tradition says, did terrible harm as a young man, using sorcery to take revenge on relatives who had cheated his mother. Full of remorse, he came to Marpa, who set him to building a stone tower, then ordered him to tear it down, then to build another, and tear that down too. Only after that did Marpa teach him. Milarepa went into the mountains, lived in caves, and sang his teaching in songs that are still sung. A wild yogi, a scholar, a farmer, a man with a past: no two alike. The lineage passes anyway, whispered from one to the next.

1281.title: The three-year retreat
1281.hook: Kagyu and other schools keep retreats of three years and three fortnights
1281.howItsDone: In the Kagyu and other Tibetan schools, practitioners enter a closed retreat of three years and three fortnights, following a daily schedule of practice sessions from before dawn into the night under a retreat teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kagyu: Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, a teaching passed by mouth. Your line was the whispered lineage.

A door closes behind a small group of people in maroon robes. On the other side is a plain retreat house: a shrine room, a kitchen, narrow rooms, a walled garden. Outside, friends and family wave. Inside, a bell rings before dawn, and a schedule begins that will run, day after day, through every season. Nobody inside will come out for a holiday or a wedding. When the door opens again, the people walking out will have spent three years and three fortnights at it. Today: the three-year retreat.
screen: `A DOOR CLOSES ON A RETREAT HOUSE.` → `A BELL BEFORE DAWN, EVERY DAY.` → `THE THREE-YEAR RETREAT.`

segments.voice: First, the length. Tradition sets the retreat at three years and three fortnights, a little more than three years. Kagyu teachers keep it, and so do other Tibetan schools. Different teachers give different reasons for the extra fortnights. What matters is that the time is fixed in advance and kept, not shortened when it gets hard. Second, what happens inside. The day runs from before dawn into the night in sessions of practice: prostrations, mantra, visualization, the teachings of the lineage, in the order a teacher lays out. Retreatants cook, clean, and keep silence for long stretches. Some Kagyu retreats include training in the practices that came down from Naropa. Third, why so long. The Kagyu school prizes practice over learning about practice: Naropa putting down his books to find the meaning, Milarepa going into the mountains and staying there. The long retreat puts that into a calendar. A teaching heard once becomes a teaching lived through every season. Fourth, the people who come out. Some go on to teach, which is part of how the whispered lineage keeps passing. Others return to their families and jobs, and carry it quietly. These retreats are kept in Tibet, India and Nepal, and in Europe and North America too. This week ran from the light of the Pure Land through the diamond vehicle, three vehicles at once, the ancient ones, hidden treasure and the whispered lineage. Today: a door, closed on purpose, for a long time.
screen: `THREE YEARS AND THREE FORTNIGHTS.` · `A DAY OF SESSIONS, BEFORE DAWN.` · `PRACTICE OVER LEARNING ABOUT IT.` · `THE PEOPLE WHO COME OUT.` · then, large: `THREE YEARS, THREE FORTNIGHTS.`

segments.voice: You don't need three years, only one small practice you could keep every day, even on your worst day: this short sit, a single bow in the morning, one breath before you eat. Choose it now, and say it to yourself once, plainly. Then do it for the length of this sit, as day one.
The three-year retreat. A Tibetan retreat of three years and three fortnights, kept by the Kagyu and other schools, with practice from before dawn into the night. Today's word.
